en: So what is a REST API then?
First of all, let me come back to just the
API term.
API stands for Application Programming
Interface, and in the end, an API always is
an interface between 2 things.
And in the context of web apps, an API,
an app that's built as an API, is basically
an interface for the client, so for the
browser and the app running in the browser
or for a mobile app to interact with your
server to fetch and send data.
So the API is basically the entry point for
HTTP requests sent by the client to the
server to then trigger certain things on the
server, for example, to store data in a
database or to fetch data.
And a REST API is simply a specific kind of
API following certain core
you could say.
REST stands for Representational State
Transfer. And in the end,
in a nutshell, a REST API is simply defined
by one key feature.
It has multiple endpoints where each
endpoint is simply a combination of a URL
with an HTTP method
that simply do different things. For
example, a REST API might expose the
/products URL for incoming POST requests
And when such a POST request is sent to
/products,
it should contain certain data in the
request body,
data that should be stored as a new product
on the server, for example. So this endpoint
always leads to product data being stored in
a database and then, for example, some
confirmation message sent back to the
client.
On the other hand, we might expose another
endpoint for GET requests to /products, so
same URL but different HTTP method.
There, since it's a GET request, no data is
attached. GET requests can't hold data.
And therefore, this would typically just
fetch data from a database and then send
that back to the client. And it's always the
same thing that happens for each endpoint
and each endpoint always needs or returns
exactly the same data. That's all part of
the REST API definition, you could say.
Now, what's interesting about the REST API
compared to the server-side rendered views
is not just that we only exchange data, but
also that we can work with more HTTP
methods.
HTTP methods,
also called HTTP verbs, give a request an
intent, you could say.
But they're not just there to give a request
an intent, they also define if a request can
carry data or not. For example.
And there are 2 very prominent HTTP methods
which every web developer should know and
which you already most likely also know by
now.
That's the GET request and the POST request.
Browsers can send GET and POST requests and
these are the only 2 HTTP methods that are
built into browsers in the sense of that you
don't need JavaScript in the browser to send
them. Instead, if you submit a form on a web
page, that form can be submitted by sending
a GET or a POST request. You can define this
with the method attribute on the form HTML
element.
And these are the only 2 requests a browser
on its own is able to send without you using
JavaScript.
And a GET request is always used if you want
